title: Coordinates and Vectors
scope: Represent position, direction, and multi-feature observations as ordered numbers.
beginnerEntry: You understand graph axes and input-output pairs.

knowledge.history: Descartes fused algebra and geometry with coordinates in 1637; Hamilton and Grassmann built vectors in the 1840s so physics could speak of force and direction. Machine learning inherited the whole toolkit: every example becomes a point, every feature list a vector, and 'similar' becomes 'nearby'.

mentalModels.name: Arrow with length and direction
mentalModels.description: A vector is an arrow: it points somewhere with a certain strength. Two numbers (the components) fully describe the arrow, and the arrow fully describes the two numbers.

mentalModels.name: Address in space
mentalModels.description: A list of coordinates is an address. With d numbers you can address any point in d-dimensional space — which is how a customer, an image, or a word becomes a point a model can work with.

analogies.analogy: GPS displacement: 3 km east and 2 km north is one arrow
analogies.whenToUse: When introducing components combining into a single direction and distance.

analogies.analogy: A shopping list of amounts (2 milk, 1 bread, 3 eggs) as a vector
analogies.whenToUse: When bridging from geometric arrows to data feature vectors.

objectives: Add and scale vectors component by component.
Connect vectors to machine-learning feature rows.

steps.prompt: Two locations are A = (2, 1) and B = (5, 5). Describe what each ordered pair means and the movement from A to B.
Why does order matter in (age, income), and what breaks if two systems reverse the positions?
Predict the result and geometric effect of adding (1, 2) to (3, 4), then multiplying (3, 4) by 2.

Play the vector experiment above: drag the arrow to point in different directions. Find a position where both components are equal, then one where a component is negative. What does a negative component mean physically?
Break it: try to describe the arrow's direction and length using a single number. What information do you lose? Why does one number per axis fix the problem?
State your discovery: a vector packages direction and magnitude as an ordered list of components, and that packaging is exactly how datasets represent every example as a point in feature space.
Coordinates locate a point relative to axes. A vector is an ordered list that can represent displacement or features; addition and scaling act on corresponding components.

Describe two walks on a city grid as vectors: 3 blocks east and 2 north is (3, 2), then (1, -4). Add them to find where you end relative to the start, and notice one place today where ordered numbers give a position: GPS, row and seat, floor and room.

A streaming service stores you as (age, weekly hours watched, titles finished), for example (29, 6, 14). You have become a point in a three-dimensional space nobody can draw, yet arithmetic handles it exactly like the city grid.
If two customers sit close together as points in feature space, they behaved similarly. What could measuring the distance between customers let a recommendation system do?
Customer A = (20, 8) and B = (60, 2) as (age, weekly visits). Predict the difference vector B - A component by component, then say in words what each component of the difference means.

Machine learning represents every observation as a feature vector. Component-wise addition, differences, and scaling work identically in 2 or 200 dimensions, so the geometry you saw on paper generalizes into spaces only arithmetic can visit.

Represent three customers as (age, monthly visits) vectors, compute one difference vector and one scaled vector, and record units and feature order beside the values. Notice the limitation: handling thousands of vectors one at a time is unmanageable. You need one structure that stores and transforms them all at once: the matrix.

experiments.title: Drag the arrow
experiments.instructions: Drag anywhere on the grid to point the arrow. Watch the (x, y) components and the magnitude update live — the arrow and the numbers are the same object.

measurement.prePrompt: Explain what (3, 7) could mean and whether changing it to (7, 3) matters.
measurement.postPrompt: For A = (2, 3), B = (6, 8), derive the displacement, scale it by one half, and map the same structure to a two-feature data record.
successCriteria: Distinguishes a point from a displacement.
Connects vectors to ordered model features.

checks.label: Reference components or coordinates per axis.
Describe vectors as representing positions or features.
Mention combining, adding, or scaling vectors.
Connect vectors to data, embeddings, or similarity.

misconceptions: A vector is only an arrow drawn on paper.
Vector addition combines all numbers into one total.
Feature vectors need no units or schema.
reasoning.tutorGuidance: Ask the learner to label every component first, calculate one component at a time, and explain whether the ordered list represents a location, a change, or an observation.
